note: Attacker-controlled bytes are accepted as the fuzz input and the last four bytes are reserved for the memory-limit helper, leaving the rest as the message payload.
The payload bytes are copied verbatim into a heap buffer that becomes the packet passed into the server parser.
The server hands the attacker-controlled packet to the chunk processor, which will decode complete OPC UA chunks from it.
The chunk header length is decoded from the input and used to decide whether the chunk is complete and should be forwarded for decoding.
A complete message body is decoded into a typed request object, so nested arrays and strings are allocated from attacker-controlled lengths and contents.
Array lengths inside the decoded request are read directly from the message and determine how much memory is allocated and how many elements are decoded.
The decoder allocates heap storage for the attacker-sized array before populating each element.
Each array element is recursively decoded, so a later element can fail after earlier elements have already been initialized.
On a partial decode failure, the decoder frees the already-initialized prefix of the array, including nested strings and structures.
String cleanup releases the byte buffer for each decoded string field as part of the array teardown.
Structure cleanup walks members and frees nested arrays/strings, so the same decoded string can be released again if the parent structure is cleared after the partial-array cleanup.

The network-message destructor clears the decoded message object after decode failure, triggering cleanup of fields that were already freed during recursive array teardown and leading to the use-after-free read reported in the crash state.
